St. Spyridon of Trimythous

St. Spyridon of Trimythous

Titles / vocation
Hierarch
Commemoration

Introduction

The OCA life describes St. Spyridon as a Cypriot shepherd with a family who later became bishop of Tremithus after his wife's death. It emphasizes his generosity, pastoral service, and received reputation as a wonderworker. The account also discusses his relics at Corfu. These narrative elements remain attributed to the published life rather than presented as independently researched episodes.

Background

St. Spyridon was a Cypriot shepherd with wife and children; the life places his episcopate after his wife’s death.

[1] Ecclesiastical saint’s life · Published life, body paragraph 1; opening: Saint Spyridon of Tremithus was born towards the end of…

Life and notable events

With respect to Spyridon, so great was his sanctity while a shepherd, that he was thought worthy of being made a Pastor of men: and having been assigned the bishopric of one of the cities in Cyprus named Trimithus, on account of his extreme humility he continued to feed his sheep during his incumbency of the bishopric. Many extraordinary things are related of him: I shall however record but one or two, lest I should seem to wander from my subject. Once about midnight, thieves having clandestinely entered his sheepfold attempted to carry off some of the sheep. But God who protected the shepherd preserved his sheep also; for the thieves were by an invisible power bound to the folds. At daybreak, when he came to the sheep and found the men with their hands tied behind them, he understood what was done: and after having prayed he liberated the thieves, earnestly admonishing and exhorting them to support themselves by honest labor, and not to take anything unjustly. He then gave them a ram, and sent them away, humorously adding, that ye may not appear to have watched all night in vain.' This is one of the miracles in connection with Spyridon.

[2] Historical church history · Socrates, Ecclesiastical History I.12; shepherd, bishop, and thieves (selected passage)

The reception which Spyridon gave to strangers will appear from the following incident. In the quadragesima, it happened that a traveler came upon a journey to visit him on one of those days in which it was his custom to keep a continuous fast with his household, and on the day appointed for tasting food, he would remain without nourishment to mid-day. Perceiving that the stranger was much fatigued, Spyridon said to his daughter, "Come, wash his feet and set meat before him." The virgin replying that there was neither bread nor barley-food in the house, for it would have been superfluous to provide such things at the time of the fast, Spyridon first prayed and asked forgiveness, and bade her to cook some salt pork which chanced to be in the house. When it was prepared, he sat down to table with the stranger, partook of the meat, and told him to follow his example. But the stranger declining, under the plea of being a Christian, he said to him, "It is for that very reason that you ought not to decline partaking of the meat; for the Divine word shows that to the pure all things are pure."

[3] Historical church history · Sozomen, Ecclesiastical History I.11; hospitality during the fast (selected passage)

The later life associates him with Nicaea and the brick sign of the Trinity.

[1] Ecclesiastical saint’s life · Published life: Nicaea tradition

Death and martyrdom

The life records repose after episcopal service, without execution or medical cause.

[1] Ecclesiastical saint’s life · Published life: repose

Writings and legacy

His relics are associated with Corfu and his remembrance with Cheesefare Saturday. Socrates and Sozomen wrote about him; no authored book is established here.

[1] Ecclesiastical saint’s life · Published life: relics and commemoration

Source context and historical limits

The identified source is a modern ecclesiastical life used in the Church’s commemoration. It transmits biographical material, received traditions, and—in some accounts—miracle narratives. Those claims remain attributed to this source; this app has not independently established a critical historical chronology or verified each miraculous episode.

A concise navigation synopsis is necessary because full reproduction rights for this modern published life have not been established. Read its complete account at the identified source; the synopsis is not a quotation.

Text checked against the identified source. No theological review is claimed.
